newsitem.title: INDIA: Depressed Indian stocks seen gaining in new year.
newsitem.headline: Depressed Indian stocks seen gaining in new year.

text.p: India's stock markets, depressed for most of 1996, are heading for better times in the new year on expectations of political stability and increased buying by institutional investors, brokers and analysts said on Friday.
"We expect a much more stable political environment and a better market in the new year," said Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive at Lloyds Securities.
On Thursday, former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao quit the key post of head of the Congress party's parliamentary group after coming under intense pressure from party members.

Rao, who spearheaded India's move away from socialist economic controls to open markets, led the country from 1991 until last May when the 111-year-old Congress party suffered its worst defeat in general elections.

The campaign to drive Rao from his last pedestal of power was part of a broader effort to revive Congress's flagging fortunes, intimately tied to Rao's manoeuvring during his last years in power and, more recently, his legal woes.
At mid-session on Friday, the Bombay share index was up 66.64 points or 2.20 percent to 3,102.50.
Indian stocks, more down than up this year, also rallied this week on the return of big local and foreign institutional investors. The Bombay bourse gained seven percent this week.
The Bombay index had fallen by 34 percent from its peak in June before the recent turnaround.
Local traders said expectations of higher allocations flowing into India in January and government resolve to tackle problems affecting the stock market also were positive factors.
Congress is the main backer of a shaky 13-party coalition government that took power last June but internal dissent in the party has constrained the market.
"With Rao's exit, we see a realignment of forces and that should see some consensus decisions being made on the economy," said Lloyds' Agarwal.
"It is a morale booster for the market... I see some sort of long-term political stability now coming up," said investment analyst Homiyar Vasania at Parag Parikh Financial Services.
Indian industry complains that Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government has done little to help depressed bourses and the flagging interest has been compounded by an economic slowdown.
In an effort to prop up the market, both Deve Gowda and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram have promised to review an unpopular corporate tax introduced in the last budget.
Analysts said the minimum alternate tax had eaten into the profits of some of India's biggest firms.
